This research study discussed both these strategies from a learner centered approach in order to determine the effectiveness of cognitive and metacognitive strategies in comprehending a reading text and building a good vocabulary. The simplest definition of metacognition, however, could be "thinking about one's thinking" or "knowing about knowing." Metacognition is actually the process in which an individual regulates one's own learning. In reading skills, specifically, metacognition would mean to think critically about your own understanding of the text as you read through. The reader needs to be aware of his or her own cognitive experience. This is especially relevant for students who are learning English in a foreign country where their only exposure to English may be in the classroom. Reading strategies have been posited as being effective in assisting EFL students overcome gaps in linguistic knowledge such as vocabulary and grammar issues. Teaching reading strategies has been recommended as an effective means of providing a student-centered learning environment which promotes learner autonomy and improves development of target language proficiency. The aim of this study is to synthesize the existing research carried out on reading strategies in EFL contexts in order to ascertain if the evidence warrants classroom time use to teach reading strategies. Using a Mixed Methods Research Synthesis, which brings together qualitative and quantitative data and then analyzes it using both qualitative and quantitative methods, the finding of thirteen studies have been synthesized. The findings suggest that the evidence is unclear whether reading strategies are an effective means for EFL students to increase their reading comprehension; there is no clear link between the frequency of reading strategies use and proficiency level; and that there is a significant difference in the types of reading strategies that high proficiency readers use compared to low proficiency readers, but it remains unclear if some strategies are more effective than others. Because the findings do not point to a particular conclusion about the effectiveness of reading strategies, it is concluded that using valuable classroom time to teach reading strategies may not be ## Mini-report: connections between strategy use and comprehension outcomes

The evidence consistently supports the idea that reading strategy instruction can improve comprehension, but the strength of the evidence and the conditions under which it works differ across sources. A direct review of studies on cognitive and metacognitive reading strategies reports that instruction is a major topic in the literature and that there is evidence of improvement in reading comprehension and vocabulary [N1-R1]. Another study explicitly states that explicit reading strategy instruction had some effect sizes for improving reading comprehension in both ESL and EFL contexts [N3-R1]. A broader review of reading strategy instruction also notes that the evidence is mixed and unclear on whether reading strategies improve reading comprehension overall, though it does find that high-proficiency readers use different types of strategies compared to low-proficiency readers [N5-F2]. This pattern suggests that strategy use is linked to improved comprehension, but the relationship is not uniformly strong or straightforward.

Evidence also shows that teaching conditions and learner factors moderate these links. The mixed-methods synthesis on EFL reading strategies found that strategy use frequency differs by proficiency level, and that the most frequently used strategies vary across high-proficiency and low-proficiency readers [N5-F2]. This implies that comprehension gains from strategy use may depend on the learner’s existing proficiency and the specific reading task. Another source notes that EFL/ESL teachers should tailor instruction to students’ reading proficiency, academic level, gender, and text type [N5-R1], reinforcing that teaching conditions and learner characteristics are important moderators.

Metacognition is integrated into the strategy framework as a higher-order cognitive component that supports strategy use and comprehension. The EFL reading strategies synthesis explicitly states that reading strategies are posited as effective in helping EFL students overcome linguistic barriers and that teaching reading strategies promotes learner autonomy and improves target-language proficiency [N5-F2]. A separate source frames reading comprehension as a process in which meaning is constructed by the learner using prior knowledge, and prior knowledge includes awareness of the subject and language use within the text, which allows readers to build inferences and make predictions [N5-F2]. The metacognitive perspective is also made explicit in the cognitive/metacognitive strategies literature: readers must monitor understanding, regulate their reading process, and use planning, active reading, and fixing-up strategies [N4-F1]. In this view, metacognition is not separate from strategy use but is part of the framework that makes strategies more effective.

In sum, the evidence links strategy use to improved comprehension, especially when instruction is explicit and when learners are supported in monitoring and regulating their reading process [N3-R1][N5-F2][N4-F1]. The links are moderated by proficiency level, text type, academic context, and other learner characteristics [N5-R1][N5-F2]. Metacognition is embedded in the framework as a regulatory component that helps learners plan, monitor, and fix up their reading [N4-F1].

## Mini-report: main categories of cognitive reading strategies in ESL/EFL

The literature on ESL/EFL reading comprehension most commonly organizes reading strategies into broad cognitive and metacognitive categories, with some sources also emphasizing linguistic and learner-specific dimensions. A review of studies on cognitive and metacognitive reading strategies explicitly identifies these two major categories as central to the literature [N1-R1][N1-R2]. The same synthesis also notes that reading strategies are classified into broader categories and that metacognition is a key element of strategy instruction [N1-R1]. A more specific framework from an EFL reading strategies synthesis divides reading strategies into types that help EFL learners overcome linguistic gaps such as vocabulary and grammar issues, and it emphasizes that effective teaching methodologies should support student-centered learning and autonomy [N5-F2]. A separate source on ESL/ESL learners notes that cognitive strategies involve attending to the language of the text, while metacognitive strategies involve monitoring the reading process [N1-R3].

Across the evidence, the most commonly used broad categories are:

1. **Cognitive strategies**: These are the direct reading behaviors learners use to process text. The literature describes them as including attention to the language, vocabulary processing, syntactic processing, and other text-based processing mechanisms [N1-R3][N5-F2]. In the metacognitive-cognitive framework, cognitive strategies are the first step in reading acquisition, where learners begin to achieve basic reading skills [N4-F1]. The synthesis also frames reading comprehension as meaning construction using prior knowledge and language awareness, which supports inferencing, prediction, and other cognitive activities [N5-F2].

2. **Metacognitive strategies**: These are higher-order regulatory strategies that help learners plan, monitor, and regulate their reading. The literature explicitly defines metacognition as “knowledge of cognition” and “regulation of cognition,” and it identifies planning, active reading strategies, and fixing-up strategies as the three elements of metacognitive reading strategies [N4-F1]. It also notes that metacognitive strategies help readers focus attention, control, and monitor the reading process [N4-F1]. In the broader review, metacognitive strategy instruction is linked to improved reading comprehension and vocabulary [N3-R3][N5-F2].

3. **Linguistic/processing strategies**: Some sources emphasize that strategies are tied to linguistic barriers and processing demands. The EFL reading strategies synthesis notes that reading strategies help EFL students overcome vocabulary and grammar issues and that reading is a process of meaning construction involving both language knowledge and subject knowledge [N5-F2]. This suggests a category of strategies that are more directly tied to decoding, vocabulary use, and syntactic processing.

How the categories differ across sources and contexts:  
- Some sources treat cognitive and metacognitive strategies as a dual taxonomy [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1].  
- Others broaden the framework to include linguistic/processing dimensions, especially in EFL contexts where vocabulary and grammar gaps are central [N5-F2][N1-R3].  
- The mixed-methods synthesis also notes that strategy use differs by proficiency level and that high-proficiency and low-proficiency readers use different types of strategies [N5-F2]. This means the same broad category may be interpreted differently depending on the learner’s proficiency, the text type, and the teaching context [N5-R1].

Overall, the main categories are cognitive, metacognitive, and linguistic/processing strategies, with the former two being the most frequently emphasized in the literature. The categorization can vary depending on whether the source is framed around strategy taxonomy, teaching effectiveness, or language-specific challenges [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F2].

The evidence identifies several frequently mentioned sub-strategies that support reading comprehension, with the most common ones being **predicting**, **inferencing**, **elaboration**, and **vocabulary-related strategies** such as lexical inferencing and guessing. A practical guide for ESL/EFL instructors states that predicting involves using knowledge of the subject matter to make predictions about content and vocabulary and to check comprehension [N2-R1]. Another source reports that proficient students used cognitive strategies such as elaboration, prediction, and inferencing to understand reading passages [N2-R2]. A related study on contextual inference notes that contextual inference, prediction, and inferencing are central to reading comprehension activities and should be emphasized in programs [N2-R3]. A lexical inferencing study explicitly investigates the effect of lexical inferencing strategies on students’ reading comprehension [N2-R4]. These examples show that the literature frequently clusters several inferential and predictive strategies together.

Why these sub-strategies are grouped together:  
- **Predicting and inferencing** are closely related because both involve using prior knowledge to anticipate or interpret meaning rather than relying only on literal text details [N2-R1][N2-R2].  
- **Elaboration and inferencing** are often grouped because they both extend understanding beyond the text surface: elaboration adds meaning, while inferencing draws conclusions from textual evidence [N2-R2].  
- **Vocabulary-related strategies** such as guessing and lexical inferencing are grouped because they address word-level difficulties that block comprehension [N2-R4].  
- The synthesis also notes that reading comprehension is built on prior knowledge and language awareness, which supports inferences, predictions, and vocabulary processing [N5-F2]. This explains why the sub-strategies are often treated as parts of a single inferential or predictive framework.

How the sub-strategies support or overlap with broader cognitive categories:  
- **Predicting and inferencing** are core to cognitive reading strategies because they involve meaning construction and active processing of text [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].  
- **Elaboration** overlaps with cognitive strategy categories by extending understanding and making connections, which is central to active reading [N2-R2].  
- **Vocabulary-related strategies** are part of the broader cognitive framework because they address language processing gaps that affect comprehension [N2-R4][N5-F2].  
- The metacognitive framework also intersects with these sub-strategies, especially through planning, active reading, and fixing-up strategies [N4-F1]. In that sense, inferential and vocabulary strategies are not only cognitive but also regulated by metacognitive control.

Limitations in the evidence:  
- The sources are not exhaustive, so some sub-strategies may be underrepresented [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R4].  
- The evidence is somewhat fragmented, with different sources emphasizing different sub-strategies and sometimes using overlapping terminology [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].  
- The relationship between sub-strategies and broader categories is clearer in some sources than in others, which means the categorization is not always fully standardized [N5-F2][N4-F1].

Overall, the most frequently identified sub-strategies are predicting, inferencing, elaboration, and lexical inferencing, and they are grouped together because they all support meaning construction, vocabulary processing, and active reading [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4]. These sub-strategies sit within the broader cognitive and metacognitive strategy framework, with metacognition helping learners plan, monitor, and fix up their reading process [N4-F1].

How the frameworks map categories and sub-strategies:  
- The **cognitive/metacognitive framework** maps reading strategies into two major categories: cognitive strategies, which are direct reading behaviors, and metacognitive strategies, which are regulatory and self-monitoring [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1]. ## Integrated final answer: how cognitive reading strategies are categorized and connected with sub-strategies

Cognitive reading strategies in ESL/EFL reading comprehension are most commonly organized around **cognitive** and **metacognitive** categories, with some sources also emphasizing **linguistic/processing** dimensions and **proficiency-based** or **text/context-based** differences [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1][N5-F2]. This taxonomy reflects a central distinction in the literature: cognitive strategies are the direct reading behaviors used to process text, while metacognitive strategies are higher-order regulatory strategies that help learners plan, monitor, and adjust their reading process [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1].

### 1) Main categories of cognitive reading strategies

The broadest and most frequently used category is **cognitive strategy**, which includes the reading behaviors learners use to understand a text. The literature defines cognitive strategies as attention to the language of the text, vocabulary processing, syntactic processing, and other text-based reading activities [N1-R3][N5-F2]. In the metacognitive-cognitive framework, cognitive strategies are described as the first step in reading acquisition, where learners achieve basic reading skills [N4-F1]. The synthesis also frames reading comprehension as a process in which meaning is constructed by the learner using prior knowledge and language awareness, which supports inferencing, prediction, and vocabulary processing [N5-F2].

The second major category is **metacognitive strategy**, which is the higher-order regulatory component of reading strategy instruction. Metacognition is defined as “knowledge of cognition” and “regulation of cognition,” and it includes planning, active reading strategies, and fixing-up strategies [N4-F1]. In this framework, metacognitive strategies help readers focus attention, control and monitor the reading process, and regulate their learning [N4-F1]. The literature also links metacognitive strategy instruction to improved reading comprehension and vocabulary [N3-R3][N5-F2].

A third, more context-specific dimension is **linguistic/processing strategy**, especially in EFL contexts where vocabulary and grammar gaps are central. The EFL reading strategies synthesis notes that reading strategies are posited as effective in helping EFL students overcome vocabulary and grammar issues and that reading is a process of meaning construction involving both language knowledge and subject knowledge [N5-F2]. This suggests that some frameworks explicitly include language-processing strategies as part of the broader strategy set.

### 2) How the categories differ across sources or contexts

The main difference across sources is whether the framework is kept simple, broadened, or adapted to learner and contextual factors.  
- Some sources treat cognitive and metacognitive strategies as a **dual taxonomy**, with cognitive strategies as direct reading behaviors and metacognitive strategies as regulatory behaviors [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1].  
- Other sources broaden the framework to include **linguistic/processing** dimensions, especially where vocabulary and grammar challenges are important [N5-F2][N1-R3].  
- Some sources emphasize **proficiency-based** differences, noting that high-proficiency and low-proficiency readers use different types of strategies [N5-F2].  
- Some sources emphasize **text and context-based** adaptation, recommending that instruction be tailored to students’ reading proficiency, academic level, gender, and text type [N5-R1][N5-F2].  
- Some sources emphasize **learner autonomy** and **strategic awareness**, framing strategy instruction as a means to promote student-centered learning and self-regulation [N5-F2].

This means the same broad category can be interpreted differently depending on the source: cognitive strategies may be understood as direct processing mechanisms in one context, while in another context they may be tied more explicitly to vocabulary or syntactic processing [N1-R3][N5-F2]. Likewise, metacognitive strategies may be treated as a higher-order regulatory component in one source, while in another they are mapped into planning, active reading, and fixing-up elements [N4-F1].

### 3) Main sub-strategies and their functions

The most frequently identified sub-strategies are **predicting**, **inferencing**, **elaboration**, and **lexical inferencing** or **vocabulary-related guessing**. A practical guide for ESL/EFL instructors states that predicting involves using knowledge of the subject matter to make predictions about content and vocabulary and to check comprehension [N2-R1]. Proficient students are reported to use cognitive strategies such as **elaboration**, **prediction**, and **inferencing** to understand reading passages [N2-R2]. Another source states that contextual inference, prediction, and inferencing are central to reading comprehension activities and should be emphasized in programs [N2-R3]. A lexical inferencing study explicitly investigates the effect of lexical inferencing strategies on students’ reading comprehension [N2-R4].

These sub-strategies are grouped together because they all support **meaning construction** and **active reading**. Predicting and inferencing are closely related because both use prior knowledge to anticipate or interpret meaning rather than relying only on literal text details [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Elaboration and inferencing are often grouped because they both extend understanding beyond the text surface: elaboration adds meaning, while inferencing draws conclusions from textual evidence [N2-R2]. Vocabulary-related strategies such as guessing and lexical inferencing are grouped because they address word-level difficulties that block comprehension [N2-R4]. The synthesis also notes that reading comprehension is built on prior knowledge and language awareness, which supports inferences, predictions, and vocabulary processing [N5-F2].

### 4) How sub-strategies overlap with broader cognitive categories

The sub-strategies overlap with broader cognitive categories in several ways.  
- **Predicting and inferencing** are core to cognitive reading strategies because they involve meaning construction and active processing of text [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].  
- **Elaboration** overlaps with cognitive strategy categories by extending understanding and making connections, which is central to active reading [N2-R2].  
- **Vocabulary-related strategies** are part of the broader cognitive framework because they address language processing gaps that affect comprehension [N2-R4][N5-F2].  
- The metacognitive framework also intersects with these sub-strategies, especially through planning, active reading, and fixing-up strategies [N4-F1]. In that sense, inferential and vocabulary strategies are not only cognitive but also regulated by metacognitive control.

### 5) Connections between strategy use and comprehension outcomes

The evidence links strategy use to improved comprehension, but the strength of the link is not uniform. A review of studies on cognitive and metacognitive reading strategies reports that instruction is a major topic in the literature and that there is evidence of improvement in reading comprehension and vocabulary [N1-R1]. Another study explicitly states that explicit reading strategy instruction had some effect sizes for improving reading comprehension in both ESL and EFL contexts [N3-R1]. A broader review of reading strategy instruction notes that the evidence is mixed and unclear whether reading strategies improve reading comprehension overall, though it does find that high-proficiency readers use different types of strategies compared to low-proficiency readers [N5-F2]. This suggests that strategy use can support comprehension, but the effect is often conditional.

Teaching conditions and learner factors moderate these links. The mixed-methods synthesis on EFL reading strategies found that strategy use frequency differs by proficiency level, and that the most frequently used strategies vary across high-proficiency and low-proficiency readers [N5-F2]. It also recommends tailoring instruction to students’ reading proficiency, academic level, gender, and text type [N5-R1]. These findings indicate that comprehension gains are often strongest when instruction is explicit, when learners are supported in monitoring and regulating their reading, and when the teaching context is adapted to the learner group.

Metacognition is integrated into the strategy framework as a regulatory component that supports comprehension. The literature frames reading comprehension as a process in which meaning is constructed by the learner using prior knowledge, and prior knowledge includes awareness of the subject and language use within the text [N5-F2]. Metacognitive strategies are described as helping readers focus attention, control and monitor the reading process, and use planning, active reading, and fixing-up strategies [N4-F1]. In other words, metacognition is not separate from strategy use: it is part of what makes strategies more effective.

### 6) ESL/EFL-specific frameworks and their limitations

The main ESL/EFL frameworks organizing reading strategies are:  
- the **cognitive/metacognitive dual taxonomy**,  
- the **proficiency-based framework**,  
- the **text/context-based framework**,  
- and the **learner-autonomy framework** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F2][N5-R1].

These frameworks map categories and sub-strategies differently. The cognitive/metacognitive framework maps reading strategies into two major categories: cognitive strategies (direct reading behaviors) and metacognitive strategies (planning, active reading, fixing-up) [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1]. The proficiency-based framework maps strategy use by learner level, noting that high-proficiency and low-proficiency readers use different types of strategies [N5-F2]. The text/context-based framework maps strategy use by text type and academic context, with instruction tailored to students’ proficiency, academic level, gender, and text type [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The learner-autonomy framework maps strategies as means to promote student-centered learning and self-regulation [N5-F2].

A limitation of these frameworks is that they are not fully standardized. Different sources emphasize different categories and sub-strategies, and terminology is sometimes inconsistent [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-F2]. The synthesis also notes that the evidence is unclear on whether reading strategies are effective overall and whether some strategies are more effective than others [N5-F2]. This creates a tension between a strong taxonomy and mixed empirical support. Another tension is that the same framework may need to be adapted depending on the learner group: high-proficiency and low-proficiency readers use different strategies, so the same framework may not fit all contexts equally [N5-F2].

### 7) Synthesis: how the categorization and sub-strategies fit together

Taken together, the literature shows that cognitive reading strategies in ESL/EFL are best understood as a **cognitive/metacognitive framework** with linguistic/processing dimensions and learner-specific adaptations [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F1][N5-F2]. Finally, metacognition is integrated into the framework not as an external add-on, but as a core regulatory component that makes strategy use more effective [N4-F1].

### Bottom line
